title: Overview of representation theory: associative algebras, representations, subrepresentations, direct sums

claims.claim: Representation theory studies representations of associative algebras.
claims.reason: This is a description of the subject's scope, not a mathematical proposition with a specified truth condition.

claims.claim: A unital associative algebra over a field is a vector space with associative bilinear multiplication and a two-sided identity.
The endomorphisms of a vector space form an associative algebra.
Algebras given by generators and relations, group algebras, and universal enveloping algebras are associative-algebra constructions.
A representation of A is a vector space V with a unital algebra homomorphism A → End(V), equivalently a left A-module.
A subrepresentation is a linear subspace invariant under every operator in the representation.
The direct sum of two representations carries the componentwise representation structure.

title: Classification of irreducible representations of U(sl(2))
notes: The classification, complemented-lattice, U(sl(2))/Lie-action preservation bridges, homogeneous-polynomial realization, and indecomposable-implies-irreducible proofs are complete.

claims.claim: Representations of U(sl(2)) may be presented equivalently as Lie action maps of sl(2).
For every positive dimension d there exists an irreducible complex sl(2)-representation of dimension d.
Any two irreducible complex sl(2)-representations of the same positive dimension d are equivalent.
The d-dimensional irreducible is realized by homogeneous polynomials of degree d-1 in x,y with h=x∂x-y∂y, e=x∂y, and f=y∂x.
Every finite-dimensional complex sl(2)-representation is completely reducible (a direct sum of irreducibles).
Every finite-dimensional indecomposable complex sl(2)-representation is irreducible.

title: Gabriel's theorem: classification of quivers of finite type by Dynkin diagrams
fidelity_note: The book explicitly says that it proves Theorem 2.1.2 only over an algebraically closed field, while a footnote states without proof that the classification remains valid over arbitrary fields. Theorem_2_1_2_general formalizes exactly the proved algebraically closed case, including loops, parallel arrows, and opposite arrows. The field-independent Dynkin-to-finite-type direction is also proved as hasFiniteRepresentationType_of_isDynkinDiagram, but no declaration assumes the unproved arbitrary-field converse. For nonempty graphs (1 ≤ n), Theorem_Dynkin_classification supplies the explicit A/D/E list rather than relying only on the predicate name IsDynkinDiagram; the scope excludes the vacuous zero-vertex bookkeeping case.

claims.claim: For connected finite quivers, finite representation type is independent of the orientation and occurs exactly when the underlying graph is Dynkin.
The finite-type classification is valid over an arbitrary field, not only an algebraically closed one.
claims.reason: The footnote asserts this stronger generalization, but the book explicitly says that it only proves the algebraically closed case. The formalization tracks the proof supplied by the book rather than introducing an unproved arbitrary-field theorem.

claims.claim: The nonempty connected Dynkin graphs are precisely A_n, D_n, E6, E7, and E8.
The listed graphs are called simply laced Dynkin diagrams.
Dynkin diagrams arise in classifications of simple Lie algebras, singularities, Platonic solids, and reflection groups.
claims.reason: This historical overview does not specify the relevant categories or a precise correspondence theorem for any of the four subjects; the exact quiver and graph classification claims are formalized separately.

title: Irreducible and indecomposable representations of k and k[x]
fidelity_note: Part (1): Etingof.Example_2_3_14_field_irreducible_unique and Etingof.Example_2_3_14_field_indecomposable_unique prove that k is the unique simple and indecomposable k-module up to linear equivalence. Part (2): the 1-dim irreducibles are classified (Example_2_3_14_polynomial_reps: simple k[x]-modules are 1-dimensional). The Jordan-block reps V_{λ,n} are built as genuine k[X]-modules (jordanRep = Module.AEval' of jordanBlock), proved indecomposable (jordanRep_indecomposable, via: every nonzero J-invariant subspace contains the eigenvector e₀) and proved not simple for n>=2 (jordanRep_not_isSimpleModule), giving the book's conclusion 'indecomposable need not be irreducible' (exists_indecomposable_not_simple, witness V_{0,2}). The completeness half is fully formalized: exists_equiv_pi_jordanRep decomposes every finite-dimensional k[X]-module over an algebraically closed field as a finite product of Jordan blocks; exists_equiv_jordanRep specializes this to show every finite-dimensional indecomposable module is one block; and jordanRep_equiv_iff shows the blocks are pairwise nonisomorphic (V_{λ,n} ≅ V_{μ,m} forces λ = μ and n = m). The route is the Mathlib structure theorem for finitely generated modules over the PID k[X] (Module.equiv_directSum_of_isTorsion) plus the cyclic model jordanQuotEquiv : k[X]/((X-λ)ⁿ) ≅ V_{λ,n}.
coverage_note: Stage 3.2 added and proved the omitted uniqueness-over-k and full finite-dimensional Jordan-decomposition claims, and unified all indecomposability statements with Definition 2.3.8.

claims.claim: For A = k, representations are vector spaces and k is the unique irreducible representation up to isomorphism.
For A = k, k is the unique indecomposable representation up to isomorphism.
Finite-dimensional irreducible k[x]-representations are one-dimensional and parameterized by the scalar action of x.
The representations V_λ are pairwise nonisomorphic.
The Jordan block J_{λ,n} has the displayed standard-basis action.
Every finite-dimensional linear operator, equivalently every finite-dimensional k[x]-module, decomposes as a finite direct sum of Jordan blocks.
The finite-dimensional indecomposable k[x]-representations are exactly the Jordan-block representations V_{λ,n}.
The Jordan-block representations V_{λ,n} are pairwise nonisomorphic, with both λ and n determined.
An indecomposable representation need not be irreducible.

title: Representations of group algebras k[G]
fidelity_note: The book claims a representation of the group algebra A = k[G] is "the same thing" as a representation of G, i.e. a vector space V with a group homomorphism rho : G -> GL(V). Formalized as two genuine bijections (Equiv), replacing the prior vacuous tautology Module k[G] V -> Module k[G] V. repEquivAlgHom: Representation k G V is equiv to (k[G] -> _a[k] Module.End k V), i.e. a representation of G is the same data as an algebra homomorphism out of k[G] (= a k-compatible k[G]-module structure on V). repEquivGL: Representation k G V is equiv to (G ->* (V ~=_l[k] V)), i.e. the same data as a group homomorphism rho : G -> GL(V) into the general linear group of invertible linear maps; invertibility is automatic because G is a group. Characterizing simp/rfl lemmas (repEquivAlgHom_apply_single, repEquivGL_apply, repEquivGL_symm_apply) pin down that the bijections are the intended maps (rho g acts as rho g), not arbitrary relabellings.
coverage_note: Stage 3.2 verified both equivalences: group-algebra representations with group representations, and group homomorphisms into endomorphisms with homomorphisms into GL(V).

claims.claim: A representation of k[G] is equivalent to a representation of G.
A representation of G is equivalently a group homomorphism G → GL(V).
GL(V) is the group of invertible linear endomorphisms and the two encodings have the same action on vectors.

claims.claim: The center Z(A) consists of elements commuting with every element of A.

On an irreducible finite-dimensional representation, every central element acts by a scalar.

title: Section 2.4 Ideals — heading and definitions

claims.claim: Left ideals, right ideals, and two-sided ideals have the stated closure conditions.
Left ideals are subrepresentations of the regular representation.
Right ideals are subrepresentations of the regular representation of the opposite algebra.
A two-sided ideal is simultaneously a left and a right ideal.
The zero ideal and the whole ring are two-sided ideals, and a nonzero ring with no others is simple.
The kernel of an algebra homomorphism is a two-sided ideal.
The two-sided ideal generated by S is the smallest such ideal and is the additive span of products a*s*b.
The left and right ideals generated by S are the corresponding one-sided spans.

title: Basis for the Weyl algebra and q-Weyl algebra
notes: Part (i): the characteristic-free theorem Proposition_2_7_1_charFree proves that {x^i y^j : i,j>=0} is a basis over every nontrivial commutative ring, using the book's faithful module E = t^a k[a][t,t^-1]. claims.claim: The ordered monomials x^i y^j for i,j >= 0 form a basis of the Weyl algebra.

coverage_note: All three contrasts of the discussion are now public theorems (#7442). title: Proof of Theorem 3.3.1 using dual representations
coverage_note: The complete advertised dual route is public: the transpose equivalence, twisted dual action, free-to-dual surjection, dual injection, regular and free-module decompositions, and final direct-sum classification are all formalized end to end.

claims.claim: Each standard V_i is irreducible; a matrix element can send any chosen nonzero vector to any target vector.
claims.note: The proof reduces to the single-factor matrix-vector calculation.

claims.claim: For finite-dimensional X, the dual X* is finite-dimensional of the same dimension.
Matrix transpose identifies Mat_d(k) with its opposite algebra because (BC)^T = C^T B^T.
Applying transpose factorwise identifies A = ⊕_i Mat_{d_i}(k) with A^op.
Using the transpose anti-automorphism, X* is again an A-representation.
A basis y_l of X* defines the A-linear map φ : A^n → X* by φ(a) = ∑_l a_l y_l.
The map φ is surjective because scalar coefficients embed from k into A.
Dualizing φ gives an injective A-linear map X → (A^n)*.
The dual of A^n is A-linearly isomorphic to A^n.
The regular representation decomposes as A ≃ ⊕_i d_i V_i.
The free representation A^n decomposes as ⊕_i (n d_i) V_i.
The image of X in A^n is a subrepresentation to which Proposition 3.1.4 applies.
Consequently X is A-linearly isomorphic to ⊕_i m_i V_i for suitable multiplicities m_i.

title: Endomorphisms of indecomposable representations are isomorphisms or nilpotent

claims.claim: Every endomorphism of a finite-dimensional indecomposable representation is either invertible or nilpotent.
The dichotomy follows from an invariant direct-sum decomposition into a nilpotent part and an invertible part.
claims.note: Lean uses the stronger arbitrary-field Fitting decomposition rather than the source's algebraically-closed generalized-eigenspace proof.

claims.claim: A finite sum of nilpotent endomorphisms of an indecomposable representation is nilpotent.
The sum result is proved inductively using the unit-or-nilpotent dichotomy and the fact that one minus a nilpotent endomorphism is invertible.

Since the theta_s sum to the identity, one theta_s is invertible; this yields an isomorphism between the first indecomposable summand and a summand of the other decomposition, with the remaining summands forming a common complement.

title: Extensions of representations and Ext^1

claims.claim: An extension of W by V may be represented on V × W by block-triangular operators with off-diagonal block f, and the zero block gives V ⊕ W.
claims.note: ExtMod carries the genuine A-module action, rather than only a family of block matrices.

claims.claim: The canonical maps V → U_f → W form a short exact sequence, and U_f/V is isomorphic to W.
The block assignment is multiplicative if and only if f satisfies f(ab)=ρ_V(a)f(b)+f(a)ρ_W(b).
The 1-cocycles form the vector space Z¹(W,V).
For X:W→V, dX(a)=ρ_V(a)X-Xρ_W(a) is a 1-cocycle.
The coboundary dX vanishes if and only if X is a homomorphism of representations.
Coboundaries form B¹(W,V)⊆Z¹(W,V), canonically isomorphic to Hom_k(W,V)/Hom_A(W,V).
claims.note: The project identifies the range and kernel of the coboundary map; Mathlib's first-isomorphism equivalence supplies the displayed quotient-to-range isomorphism.

claims.claim: Ext¹(W,V) is the quotient Z¹(W,V)/B¹(W,V).
If f-f' is a coboundary, then the corresponding extensions U_f and U_f' are isomorphic.
A unitriangular extension isomorphism U_f≅U_f' implies f-f' is a coboundary.
For finite-dimensional irreducible V,W over the algebraically closed base field, U_f≅U_f' exactly when their Ext¹ classes are proportional.
claims.note: The theorem uses a nonzero scalar and equality modulo B¹, which is precisely equality of projective Ext¹ classes.

claims.claim: Nontrivial extensions are parametrized by ℙExt¹(W,V), and every extension splits if and only if Ext¹(W,V)=0.

claims.claim: Cl(V) is the tensor algebra modulo v⊗v-(v,v)1, equivalently the Clifford algebra of Q(v)=B(v,v).

For the zero bilinear form, Cl(V) is the exterior algebra ΛV.
Ordered Clifford monomials indexed by subsets span and form a 2^dim(V)-element basis, so dim Cl(V)=2^dim(V).
If B is nondegenerate, then Cl(V) is semisimple.
If dim V=2n and B is nondegenerate, Cl(V) is a full matrix algebra End(S) with dim S=2^n, hence has one irreducible representation of that dimension.

claims.claim: For irreducible finite-dimensional V and W, density makes A → End(V) and B → End(W) surjective.
The resulting tensor-product action reaches enough endomorphisms of V ⊗ W to make V ⊗ W irreducible.
For the finite-dimensional image algebras A' and B' in End(M), Rad(A' ⊗ B') = Rad(A') ⊗ B' + A' ⊗ Rad(B').
M carries the induced A' ⊗ B' action, so replacing A and B by their image algebras loses no information and one may assume without loss of generality that A and B are finite dimensional.
For finite-dimensional A and B over an algebraically closed field, Rad(A ⊗ B) = Rad(A) ⊗ B + A ⊗ Rad(B).
J = Rad(A) ⊗ B + A ⊗ Rad(B) is a nilpotent ideal and hence J ⊆ Rad(A ⊗ B).
The quotient (A ⊗ B)/J is isomorphic to (A/Rad(A)) ⊗ (B/Rad(B)).
The tensor product of the two finite-dimensional semisimple radical quotients is semisimple over an algebraically closed field.
Semisimplicity of the quotient gives Rad(A ⊗ B) ⊆ J, completing the radical equality.
Consequently (A ⊗ B)/Rad(A ⊗ B) is isomorphic to (A/Rad(A)) ⊗ (B/Rad(B)).
An irreducible M over the semisimple quotient has the form V ⊗ W with irreducible factor representations.
The factors V and W are uniquely determined by M.

title: Maschke's theorem
fidelity_note: [fidelity #5656] VERIFIED. Book part (ii)'s explicit algebra isomorphism, its compatibility with the left regular G-actions, the isotypic regular-representation decomposition, and the sum-of-squares formula are exposed respectively by Etingof.Theorem4_1_1_algebra_iso, Etingof.Theorem4_1_1_regularRep_iso, Etingof.Theorem4_1_1_regularRep_isotypic, and Etingof.Theorem4_1_1_sum_of_squares.

claims.claim: The hypotheses are a finite group G and a field k whose characteristic does not divide |G|.
The group algebra k[G] is semisimple.
The V_i form a finite, pairwise non-isomorphic, exhaustive family of irreducible representations of G.
There is a k-algebra isomorphism ψ : k[G] → ⊕_i End(V_i).
On a group element g, the i-th component of ψ(g) is the action of g on V_i.
The algebra isomorphism ψ is also an isomorphism of G-representations when both sides carry left multiplication.
The regular representation decomposes as the direct sum of dim(V_i) copies of each irreducible V_i.
The dimensions of the irreducible representations satisfy |G| = ∑_i dim(V_i)^2.
The semisimple-algebra structure theorem derives the algebra decomposition and dimension consequences from semisimplicity.
To prove semisimplicity, it suffices to give every subrepresentation an invariant complementary subrepresentation.
Every vector subspace W of V admits a vector-space complement and hence a projection P onto W along that complement.
The projection P is the identity on W, vanishes on the chosen complement, and has that complement as its kernel.
Averaging the conjugates of P over G and dividing by |G| produces the operator P̄ used in Maschke's proof.
The averaged operator restricts to the identity on W and has image contained in W, so it is a projection.
Reindexing the group sum proves that the averaged projection is G-equivariant.
The kernel W' of the averaged projection is an invariant complement, yielding V = W ⊕ W' as representations.

note: Formalized (issue #5654, epic #5338) in Chapter5/Remark5_2_8.lean, replacing the earlier doc-only false closure. The remark is an alternative proof of the vanishing statement of Problem 5.2.7(b), decomposing into five steps. Three are formalized as real sorry-free theorems: Step 1 (pow_coprime_bijective) g ↦ gʲ is a bijection G → G for gcd(|G|,j)=1; Step 2 (prod_ne_one_pow) reindexing the product over G∖{1} along that bijection gives ∏_{g≠1} f(gʲ) = ∏_{g≠1} f(g), i.e. ∏_{g≠1}|χ_V(gʲ)|² = β; Step 5 + contradiction (not_isIntegral_rat_mem_Ioo) no rational algebraic integer lies in (0,1), built on Etingof.Proposition5_2_5. Also formalized sorry-free: the algebraic-integer half (isIntegral_prod_normSq_character, β is a product of algebraic integers) and the root-of-unity content of Step 3 (character_eq_sum_rootsOfUnity: each χ_V(g) is a sum of N-th roots of unity, N=|G|, since the eigenvalues of ρ(g) are roots of its charpoly and ρ(g) has order dividing N — placing β in ℚ(ζ_N)). Step 4 (representation-theoretic core) is now formalized sorry-free (#5772): character_ringHom_pow proves σ(χ_V(g)) = χ_V(gʲ) for any ring endomorphism σ of ℂ raising every N-th root of unity to its j-th power, via the trace-power-sum trace_pow_eq_sum_eigenvalues (ρ(g) is semisimple as its minpoly divides squarefree X^N-1, so V splits into eigenspaces and trace(ρ(g)ᵏ)=∑_μ (dim Eμ)·μᵏ); combined with Step 2, ringHom_prod_char_inv gives σ(β)=β for β=∏_{g≠1} χ_V(g)·χ_V(g⁻¹). The field-theoretic half of Step 4 together with Step 3 (β∈ℚ) is now formalized sorry-free (#5772): character_prod_rat realizes the cyclotomic field K=ℚ(ζ_N) as the intermediate field ℚ⟮ζ⟯⊆ℂ for a primitive N-th root ζ, lifts β to β_K∈K (each character value is a ℤ-combination of N-th roots of unity, all lying in K), shows β_K is fixed by the whole Galois group Gal(K/ℚ) (each automorphism raises roots of unity to a fixed power ζ↦ζʲ via IsPrimitiveRoot.autToPow_spec, so φ(χ_V(g))=χ_V(gʲ) after transporting the eigenvalue decomposition into K, and reindexing along g↦gʲ restores the product), and concludes β_K∈ℚ from IsGalois.mem_range_algebraMap_iff_fixed (fixed field of the full Galois group is the base field). All five steps are composed into the capstone beta_rat_not_mem_Ioo (Remark 5.2.8, assembled): given the rational q with algebraMap ℚ ℂ q = β from character_prod_rat, and the bound 0<q<1, it derives False — β is a product of algebraic integers (FDRep.character_isIntegral), hence a rational algebraic integer, so not_isIntegral_rat_mem_Ioo applies. The one hypothesis not established in this file is 0<β<1, the main argument of Problem 5.2.7(b) (a separate item), taken as a hypothesis by the capstone.
